interview.a: To keep tests fast, deterministic and independent of network or third-party availability.

topics.title: Packaging and Project Structure
topics.summary: Structure a project, declare dependencies in pyproject.toml and build distributable packages.
topics.description:
Good structure and packaging make a project installable, testable and shareable.

### Recommended layout
```text
myproject/
  pyproject.toml
  README.md
  src/
    mypkg/
      __init__.py
      core.py
  tests/
    test_core.py
```
The `src/` layout prevents accidentally importing the local folder instead of the installed package.

### pyproject.toml
The modern single configuration file (PEP 517/518/621):
```toml
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=68"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "mypkg"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = ["requests>=2.31"]

[project.scripts]
mytool = "mypkg.cli:main"
```

### Workflow
- `pip install -e .` installs in editable mode while developing.
- `python -m build` creates a wheel and sdist; `twine upload dist/*` publishes to PyPI.
- Entry points under `[project.scripts]` create command-line tools.

### Dependency tools
`pip` + `venv`, **Poetry**, **uv**, **pipenv**, **pip-tools**. They resolve and lock versions so installs are reproducible.

### Quality tooling
`ruff` (lint + format), `black`, `mypy`, `pre-commit`, `pytest`, plus CI (GitHub Actions) running them on each push.

### Versions
Use semantic versioning; pin application dependencies exactly, but give libraries loose ranges.
keyPoints: pyproject.toml is the modern standard config file
Use src/ layout and pip install -e . during development
python -m build creates a wheel and sdist
Entry points create CLI commands
Lock dependencies for reproducible installs
pitfalls: Committing virtual environments or secrets
Unpinned dependencies breaking production later
Importing from the working directory instead of the installed package

topics.title: Scraping Basics, Ethics and robots.txt
topics.summary: What web scraping is, when it is allowed, and how to respect robots.txt and site rules.
topics.description:
**Web scraping** means fetching web pages with a program and extracting the data you need (prices, headlines, listings). Typical uses are price comparison, research datasets, monitoring and lead generation.

### The scraping pipeline
1. **Fetch** the page (HTTP request or a browser).
2. **Parse** the HTML (or JSON) into a structure.
3. **Extract** the fields you want.
4. **Store** them (CSV, JSON, database).

### Before you scrape: ethics and legality
- Check whether the site has an **official API** or downloadable dataset; that is always better.
- Read the **Terms of Service**; some sites forbid automated access.
- Respect **`robots.txt`** (`https://site.com/robots.txt`), which lists paths crawlers should avoid and sometimes a `Crawl-delay`. It is not a security feature, but ignoring it is bad practice.
- Do not overload servers: add delays, limit concurrency, cache pages.
- Identify yourself with a meaningful `User-Agent` where appropriate.
- Never scrape private or login-protected personal data, and be careful with copyrighted content and personal information (GDPR and similar laws).
- Do not bypass paywalls or CAPTCHAs.

### Good citizen checklist
Cache responses on disk while developing so you do not hit the server repeatedly, scrape off-peak, back off when you get 429 or 5xx responses and stop if asked.

Python's standard library includes `urllib.robotparser`, which answers "is this URL allowed for my bot?".
keyPoints: Prefer official APIs over scraping
Read robots.txt and the Terms of Service first
Throttle requests and cache while developing
Do not collect personal or protected data carelessly
Fetch, parse, extract, store is the basic pipeline
pitfalls: Hammering a server with rapid parallel requests
Assuming public means free to reuse commercially
Ignoring robots.txt and getting your IP blocked

examples.title: Check robots.txt rules with the standard library
examples.code:
from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser

robots_txt = """
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /search
Crawl-delay: 5

User-agent: BadBot
Disallow: /
"""

rp = RobotFileParser()
rp.parse(robots_txt.splitlines())

print(rp.can_fetch("MyScraper", "https://shop.test/products/1"))
print(rp.can_fetch("MyScraper", "https://shop.test/admin/users"))
print(rp.can_fetch("BadBot", "https://shop.test/products/1"))
print("crawl delay:", rp.crawl_delay("MyScraper"))
examples.explanation: In real code use rp.set_url(".../robots.txt") then rp.read() to download the file.

interview.a: It depends on the site terms, the type of data, copyright, privacy laws and jurisdiction. Public data is often scrapable, but you must respect terms, avoid personal data abuse and not harm the service.

topics.title: HTTP Basics for Scrapers
topics.summary: Requests, responses, methods, status codes, headers and URLs: the protocol you scrape over.
topics.description:
Scraping is just automating what a browser does over **HTTP**. Understanding it makes debugging much easier.

### Request
- **Method**: `GET` (fetch), `POST` (send data), also `PUT`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`.
- **URL**: scheme, host, path, query string (`?q=python&page=2`), fragment.
- **Headers**: metadata such as `User-Agent`, `Accept`, `Cookie`, `Referer`.
- **Body**: form data or JSON for POST.

### Response
- **Status code**: `200` OK, `301/302` redirect, `403` forbidden (often bot detection), `404` not found, `429` too many requests, `500+` server errors.
- **Headers**: `Content-Type`, `Set-Cookie`, `Retry-After`.
- **Body**: HTML, JSON, images, etc.

### Useful URL tools
`urllib.parse` splits and builds URLs: `urlparse`, `urljoin` (turn relative links absolute), `urlencode`, `parse_qs`.

### Statelessness and cookies
HTTP is stateless; sites keep you "logged in" by sending a **cookie** which the client returns on every request.

### Inspecting traffic
Open your browser **DevTools -> Network** tab. You can see exactly which request returns the data, its headers and payload; this is the single most useful scraping skill, because often the data comes from a hidden JSON endpoint.

### HTTPS and timeouts
Always set a **timeout**; a request without one can hang forever.
keyPoints: GET fetches, POST sends data
2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
Headers carry User-Agent, cookies and content type
Use urljoin to resolve relative links
DevTools Network tab shows the real requests
pitfalls: Not setting a timeout
Building URLs by string concatenation instead of urlencode
Ignoring 403/429 and retrying immediately

examples.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse, urljoin, urlencode, parse_qs

url = "https://shop.test/products/list?category=books&page=2#top"
parts = urlparse(url)
print(parts.scheme, parts.netloc, parts.path)
print(parse_qs(parts.query))

print(urljoin("https://shop.test/products/list", "item-5.html"))
print(urljoin("https://shop.test/products/list", "/cart"))

params = {"q": "python web scraping", "page": 3}
print("https://shop.test/search?" + urlencode(params))

interview.a: Too Many Requests: you are being rate limited. Slow down and respect the Retry-After header.

interview.q: Why does a scraper often get 403 while the browser works?
interview.a: The server detects non-browser traffic from missing or unusual headers, cookies, TLS fingerprint or IP reputation.

topics.title: The requests Library
topics.summary: Fetch pages and APIs with requests: GET, params, headers, timeouts, errors and JSON.
topics.description:
`requests` is the most popular HTTP client for Python. Install with `pip install requests`.

### Core usage
```python
import requests

r = requests.get("https://example.com", timeout=10)
r.status_code      # 200
r.text             # decoded HTML string
r.content          # raw bytes
r.json()           # parsed JSON
r.headers          # response headers
r.url              # final URL after redirects
r.raise_for_status()  # raises HTTPError for 4xx/5xx
```

### Passing data
- Query string: `requests.get(url, params={"q": "python"})`
- Headers: `headers={"User-Agent": "..."}`
- Form POST: `requests.post(url, data={...})`
- JSON POST: `requests.post(url, json={...})`
- Files: `files={"file": open("a.png", "rb")}`

### Error handling
Network failures raise `requests.exceptions.RequestException` subclasses (`Timeout`, `ConnectionError`, `HTTPError`). Wrap calls in `try/except` and **always pass `timeout=`**.

### Retries
Mount an `HTTPAdapter` with `urllib3.util.Retry` on a `Session` to retry automatically with backoff on 429/5xx.

### Encoding
`r.encoding` is guessed from headers; if text looks garbled set `r.encoding = r.apparent_encoding`.

### Limits
`requests` is synchronous and does not run JavaScript. For many concurrent requests use threads or `httpx`/`aiohttp`; for JavaScript pages use a browser tool.
keyPoints: requests.get(url, params=, headers=, timeout=)
raise_for_status() turns HTTP errors into exceptions
r.json() parses JSON; r.text is the decoded body
Always set a timeout
It does not execute JavaScript
pitfalls: No timeout, so the script hangs forever
Treating a 200 response as valid data without checking the content
Using r.text when the response is binary

Retries with backoff
examples.code:
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry

session = requests.Session()
retry = Retry(
    total=3,
    backoff_factor=1,                      # 1s, 2s, 4s
    status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
)
session.mount("https://", HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry))
resp = session.get("https://httpbin.org/status/200", timeout=10)
print(resp.status_code)

interview.q: Why must you pass timeout to requests?
interview.a: requests has no default timeout, so a stalled connection can block your program indefinitely.

topics.title: BeautifulSoup: Parsing HTML
topics.summary: Parse HTML into a tree and find tags with find, find_all, attributes and navigation.
topics.description:
**BeautifulSoup** (package `beautifulsoup4`, import `bs4`) turns messy HTML into a navigable tree. It is forgiving of broken markup and perfect for small to medium scraping jobs.

```bash
pip install requests beautifulsoup4 lxml
```

### Creating the soup
```python
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml")      # or "html.parser" (built in)
```
`lxml` is faster; `html.parser` needs no extra install.

### Finding elements
- `soup.find("h1")` first match or `None`.
- `soup.find_all("a", class_="link", limit=10)` list of matches.
- Filters: `id="x"`, `class_="y"` (note underscore), `attrs={"data-id": "5"}`, `string=re.compile(...)`.
- Navigation: `.parent`, `.children`, `.next_sibling`, `.find_next("p")`.

### Reading data
- `tag.get_text(strip=True)` or `.text` for text.
- `tag["href"]` or `tag.get("href")` for attributes (use `get` to avoid `KeyError`).
- `tag.attrs` dict of all attributes.

### Defensive extraction
Elements often vanish. Check for `None` before calling methods:
```python
price_tag = item.find("span", class_="price")
price = price_tag.get_text(strip=True) if price_tag else None
```

### Remember
BeautifulSoup only sees the HTML the server sent. If data is missing, it is probably rendered by JavaScript (see the JS-rendered pages topic).

find returns one tag or None; find_all returns a list
Use class_ (with underscore) to filter by CSS class

Always guard against missing elements
pitfalls: Calling .text on None when an element is missing
Using the wrong parser name or forgetting to install lxml
Expecting JavaScript-generated content to appear

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = """

Python Book

Rs 499 Details

Flask Guide

Details
""" soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser") for item in soup.find_all("div", class_="product"): title = item.find("h2", class_="title").get_text(strip=True) price_tag = item.find("span", class_="price") price = price_tag.get_text(strip=True) if price_tag else "n/a" link = item.find("a")["href"] print(item["data-id"], title, price, link)

interview.q: Which parser should you use with BeautifulSoup?
interview.a: lxml for speed, html.parser if you want no dependency, html5lib for the most browser-like parsing of very broken HTML.

topics.title: CSS Selectors in Scraping
topics.summary: Use select() and select_one() to target elements with the same selectors you know from CSS.
topics.description:
If you know CSS you already know how to locate elements. BeautifulSoup's `select()` and `select_one()` accept **CSS selectors**, which are often shorter and more readable than chained `find` calls. Scrapy, Playwright, Selenium and `parsel` use the same syntax. ### Selector cheat sheet | Selector | Meaning | |---|---| | `p` | all `

` | | `.price` | class `price` | | `#main` | id `main` | | `div.card > h2` | `h2` direct child of `div.card` | | `ul li a` | any `a` inside `li` inside `ul` | | `a[href]` | has `href` | | `a[href^="http"]` | href starts with | | `a[href$=".pdf"]` | href ends with | | `a[href*="product"]` | href contains | | `li:nth-child(2)` | second child | | `h2 + p` | `p` immediately after `h2` | | `h2, h3` | either | ### BeautifulSoup ```python soup.select("div.product h2.title") # list soup.select_one("li.next a") # first or None [a["href"] for a in soup.select("a[href]")] ``` ### Scrapy / parsel Scrapy adds pseudo-elements: `::text` and `::attr(href)`, with `.get()` and `.getall()`. ```python response.css("div.quote span.text::text").getall() ``` ### Tips - Prefer stable hooks (ids, semantic classes, `data-*` attributes) over deep positional selectors; layout changes break `div > div > div:nth-child(3)`. - Test selectors live in DevTools: `document.querySelectorAll("...")` in the console.

Scrapy adds ::text and ::attr(name)
Prefer stable classes and data attributes
Test selectors in the browser console first

Forgetting select() returns a list even for one match
Using utility class names generated at build time (they change)

  • Alpha

    10.5

  • Beta

    8.0

interview.q: When prefer CSS selectors over XPath?
interview.a: For most cases: they are shorter and familiar. XPath is needed for upward navigation (parent/ancestor) and text-based conditions.

interview.a: Use the ::attr(name) pseudo-element, e.g. response.css("a::attr(href)").getall().

topics.title: lxml and XPath
topics.summary: Query HTML with XPath expressions for powerful and fast extraction.
topics.description:
**lxml** is a fast C-based parser. Its main strength is **XPath**, a query language for navigating a document tree. XPath can do things CSS cannot: select by text, walk to parents and ancestors, and use functions and conditions.

```python
from lxml import html
tree = html.fromstring(page_html)
titles = tree.xpath("//h2[@class='title']/text()")
```

### XPath essentials
| Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `//a` | all `a` anywhere |
| `/html/body/div` | absolute path |
| `//div[@id='main']` | attribute equals |
| `//a/@href` | attribute value |
| `//p/text()` | text nodes |
| `//li[1]` | first li (1-based) |
| `//a[contains(@href, 'product')]` | contains |
| `//a[starts-with(@href, 'http')]` | starts with |
| `//span[text()='Price']/following-sibling::span` | relative move |
| `//td/..` | parent |
| `//*[@class and @id]` | any element with both |

### Return types
`xpath()` always returns a **list**: elements, strings or numbers depending on the expression.

### Relative XPath
When looping over items, start the inner expression with a dot: `item.xpath(".//span[@class='price']/text()")`. Without the dot it searches the whole document.

### Class matching
`@class='card'` matches only the exact attribute value. For multi-class elements use `contains(concat(' ', normalize-space(@class), ' '), ' card ')`.

### Where else
Scrapy: `response.xpath(...)`. Selenium: `By.XPATH`. Playwright: `page.locator("xpath=...")`.

xpath() returns a list
Use .// when searching inside an element
XPath indexes start at 1
contains(), starts-with() and normalize-space() are the workhorses
pitfalls: Forgetting the leading dot in a relative expression
Using 0-based indexes
Exact @class match failing when an element has several classes

from lxml import html page = """
NameLaptop
Price52,000
  • First
  • Second
""" tree = html.fromstring(page) price = tree.xpath("//td[text()='Price']/following-sibling::td/text()") print(price) # ['52,000'] for li in tree.xpath("//li[contains(@class, 'item')]"): text = li.xpath("string(.//a)") href = li.xpath(".//a/@href")[0] print(text, href) print(tree.xpath("//li[1]/a/@href"))

interview.q: When is XPath better than CSS selectors?
interview.a: When you need to select by text content, walk up to a parent or ancestor, or use position and functions in conditions.

interview.q: Why do XPath expressions inside a loop start with a dot?
interview.a: The dot makes the path relative to the current element; without it the expression searches from the document root.

topics.title: Pagination and Crawling Multiple Pages
topics.summary: Walk through numbered pages, next links, offsets and infinite scroll while staying polite.
topics.description:
Real sites split results over many pages. There are a few common patterns.

### 1. Numbered URLs
`https://site.com/list?page=1`, `/page/2/`. Loop while pages return results:
```python
page = 1
while True:
    items = scrape(f"{BASE}?page={page}")
    if not items:
        break
    page += 1
```

### 2. "Next" link
Find the next-page anchor and follow it until it disappears. This is robust because you do not need to know the page count. Always convert relative hrefs with `urljoin`.

### 3. Offset / limit APIs
`?offset=40&limit=20`. Increase `offset` by `limit` until the response is empty or fewer than `limit` items arrive.

### 4. Infinite scroll / "load more"
The page loads data from a background JSON request. Open DevTools -> Network -> Fetch/XHR, scroll and copy that endpoint; then paginate the API directly. If that is impossible, drive a browser and scroll.

### 5. Cursor-based
The response contains `next_cursor` or `has_next`; pass it into the next request.

### Safety rules
- Add `time.sleep(1)` or random delay between pages.
- Set a **maximum page** limit to avoid infinite loops.
- Track visited URLs in a `set` to avoid cycles.
- Save progress so you can resume after failure.
- Deduplicate items by a stable id.
keyPoints: Detect the pattern: page numbers, next link, offset or cursor
Follow the next link instead of guessing the page count
Resolve relative URLs with urljoin
Add delays, a page cap and a visited set
Infinite scroll usually hides a JSON API
pitfalls: Endless loops when the site keeps returning the last page
Skipping urljoin and breaking on relative links
No delay between pages

examples.title: Follow the next link
examples.code:
import time
import requests
from urllib.parse import urljoin
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def crawl(start_url, max_pages=5):
    url, seen, results = start_url, set(), []
    while url and url not in seen and len(seen) < max_pages:
        seen.add(url)
        r = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()
        soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, "lxml")
        for q in soup.select("div.quote"):
            results.append({
                "text": q.select_one("span.text").get_text(strip=True),
                "author": q.select_one("small.author").get_text(strip=True),
            })
        nxt = soup.select_one("li.next > a")
        url = urljoin(url, nxt["href"]) if nxt else None
        time.sleep(1)                          # be polite
    return results

data = crawl("https://quotes.toscrape.com/")
print(len(data), data[0])

interview.a: Find the XHR/fetch request that loads more data in the Network tab and call that API with increasing page, offset or cursor values; otherwise scroll with a browser automation tool.

interview.a: Keep a set of visited URLs, cap the maximum number of pages and stop when a page yields no new items.

topics.title: Sessions, Cookies and Headers
topics.summary: Maintain state across requests, log in, reuse connections and send realistic headers.
topics.description:
### Why sessions?
A `requests.Session` keeps **cookies** and default headers across requests and reuses TCP connections, which is faster. It is how you stay logged in and behave like one browser visitor.

```python
s = requests.Session()
s.headers.update({"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 ...", "Accept-Language": "en-US,en;q=0.9"})
s.get(home_url)                               # receives cookies
s.post(login_url, data={"user": "a", "pw": "b"})
s.get(profile_url)                            # cookie sent automatically
```

### Cookies
`s.cookies.get_dict()` shows them. You can set your own: `s.cookies.set("sessionid", "abc")`. If a site shows content only after login, copy the cookie from DevTools for a quick test (only for your own account).

### Headers worth setting
- `User-Agent`: the default `python-requests/x.y` is often blocked.
- `Accept`, `Accept-Language`: look like a browser.
- `Referer`: some sites check where the click came from.
- `Authorization`: tokens for APIs (`Bearer <token>`).
- `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest` for some AJAX endpoints.

### CSRF tokens
Login forms often include a hidden `csrf` input. Load the form page first, extract the token with BeautifulSoup and send it with the POST.

### Authentication types
Basic (`auth=("user", "pass")`), token/Bearer headers, cookies from form login, and OAuth for official APIs.

Only log in with your own accounts and where the terms allow it.
keyPoints: Session persists cookies and headers
Set a realistic User-Agent and Accept headers
Fetch the login page first to get CSRF tokens
Use Authorization headers for API tokens
Sessions also reuse connections for speed
pitfalls: Using the default python-requests User-Agent
Forgetting the hidden CSRF field on login
Hard-coding secrets in code instead of environment variables

import os
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

BASE = "https://quotes.toscrape.com"
s = requests.Session()
s.headers.update({"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; CodeReviseBot/1.0)"})

login_page = s.get(f"{BASE}/login", timeout=10)
soup = BeautifulSoup(login_page.text, "lxml")
token = soup.select_one("input[name=csrf_token]")["value"]

resp = s.post(f"{BASE}/login", timeout=10, data={
    "csrf_token": token,
    "username": os.environ["SITE_USER"],
    "password": os.environ["SITE_PASS"],
})
print(resp.status_code, "Logout" in resp.text)
print(s.cookies.get_dict())

page = s.get(f"{BASE}/", timeout=10)      # still logged in

interview.a: It keeps cookies and headers between calls and reuses connections, so you can stay logged in and run faster.

interview.q: What is a CSRF token and how does it affect scrapers?
interview.a: A hidden random value tied to the session that the server expects in form posts; scrapers must fetch the form first and send the token back.

topics.title: APIs vs Scraping and JavaScript-Rendered Pages
topics.summary: Prefer APIs and hidden JSON endpoints; know why HTML is sometimes empty and how to handle it.
topics.description:
### Official APIs first
An API returns structured JSON designed for programs: stable, fast and legally clearer. Check the site footer or docs for "API", "developers" or "RSS". With APIs you deal with **keys, rate limits and pagination** instead of HTML.

| | API | HTML scraping |
|---|---|---|
| Stability | high, versioned | breaks on redesign |
| Speed | fast, small payload | heavier |
| Data shape | clean JSON | you must parse |
| Permission | explicit | grey area |

### Why is my HTML empty?
Many modern sites (React, Vue, Angular) send a nearly empty HTML shell and build the page in the browser with JavaScript. `requests` only gets the shell. "View Source" shows what `requests` sees; "Inspect Element" shows the rendered DOM.

### Three ways to handle JS-rendered pages
1. **Find the hidden API (best).** DevTools -> Network -> Fetch/XHR. Reload the page, look for JSON responses, then call that URL with `requests`. It is fast and returns clean data.
2. **Look for embedded JSON.** Many pages ship data in `<script id="__NEXT_DATA__">` or `application/ld+json`. Parse it with `json.loads`.
3. **Use a real browser.** Selenium or Playwright execute the JavaScript and give you the final HTML. Slower and heavier, so use only when 1 and 2 fail.

### Headless browsers and rendering services
Browsers can run **headless** (no window). Hosted rendering services also exist, but they cost money and add latency.
keyPoints: Prefer official APIs, then hidden JSON endpoints

Check for embedded JSON in script tags
Use Selenium or Playwright only when needed

Copying a short-lived token from DevTools into long-term code

while True:
    r = requests.get(API, params={"page": page}, timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = r.json()

    if not data["has_next"]:
        break
    page += 1

print(len(quotes))
print(quotes[0]["author"]["name"], "-", quotes[0]["text"][:40])

interview.a: The content is rendered client-side by JavaScript. Fetch the underlying XHR/JSON endpoint, read embedded JSON, or use a headless browser.

interview.q: Why is an API better than scraping?
interview.a: Stable structured data, faster, lighter and explicitly permitted, so far less maintenance than HTML parsing.

topics.title: Selenium Browser Automation
topics.summary: Drive a real browser to click, type, wait and scrape JavaScript-heavy pages.
topics.description:
**Selenium** controls a real browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) from Python. Because the browser executes JavaScript, you can scrape anything a user can see, fill in forms, click buttons and take screenshots. It is also widely used for UI testing.

```bash
pip install selenium
```
Selenium 4.6+ includes **Selenium Manager**, which downloads the matching browser driver automatically.

### Basic flow
```python
driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=opts)
driver.get(url)
elements = driver.find_elements(By.CSS_SELECTOR, ".quote")
driver.quit()
```

### Locators
`By.ID`, `By.CSS_SELECTOR`, `By.XPATH`, `By.NAME`, `By.CLASS_NAME`, `By.LINK_TEXT`. `find_element` returns one (raises `NoSuchElementException`), `find_elements` returns a list (possibly empty).

### Waiting (very important)
Pages load asynchronously, so use **explicit waits** instead of `time.sleep`:
```python
WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(
    EC.presence_of_element_located((By.CSS_SELECTOR, ".quote"))
)
```
Other conditions: `visibility_of_element_located`, `element_to_be_clickable`.

### Actions
`element.click()`, `send_keys("text")`, `element.text`, `get_attribute("href")`, `driver.execute_script("window.scrollTo(0, document.body.scrollHeight)")` for infinite scroll, `driver.page_source` to hand HTML to BeautifulSoup.

### Headless
`--headless=new` runs without a window. Always call `driver.quit()` in a `finally` block to avoid orphan browser processes.
keyPoints: Selenium controls a real browser and runs JavaScript
Use explicit waits (WebDriverWait) instead of sleep

Leaving browser processes running after errors
Using Selenium for pages that have a simple JSON API

from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By
from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait
from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC

opts = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
opts.add_argument("--headless=new")
opts.add_argument("--window-size=1280,900")

driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=opts)
try:
    driver.get("https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/")
    WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(
        EC.presence_of_element_located((By.CSS_SELECTOR, "div.quote"))
    )
    for q in driver.find_elements(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "div.quote"):
        text = q.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "span.text").text
        author = q.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "small.author").text
        print(author, "-", text[:50])

    nxt = driver.find_elements(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "li.next a")
    if nxt:
        nxt[0].click()
finally:
    driver.quit()

interview.a: They wait only until a condition is true (up to a timeout), making scripts both faster and more reliable than fixed sleeps.

interview.q: When would you choose Selenium over requests?
interview.a: When the content needs JavaScript execution, user interaction (clicks, forms, scrolling) or complex login flows.

topics.title: Playwright for Python
topics.summary: A modern, fast browser automation library with auto-waiting, great selectors and network control.
topics.description:
**Playwright** (from Microsoft) automates Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. Compared with Selenium it has **auto-waiting** (actions wait until elements are ready), a cleaner API, built-in tracing and easy interception of network requests. It has sync and async Python APIs.

```bash
pip install playwright
playwright install chromium
```

### Sync API
```python
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True)
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/")
    page.wait_for_selector("div.quote")
    print(page.locator("span.text").all_inner_texts())
    browser.close()
```

### Locators
`page.locator("css=...")`, `page.get_by_text("Next")`, `page.get_by_role("button", name="Login")`, `page.get_by_placeholder(...)`. Locators are lazy and re-evaluated on each action, which makes scripts stable.

### Actions
`click()`, `fill("text")`, `press("Enter")`, `select_option()`, `inner_text()`, `get_attribute("href")`, `page.screenshot(path="a.png")`, `page.content()` for the HTML.

### Superpowers for scraping
- **Intercept responses**: `page.on("response", handler)` to capture the JSON API calls the page makes.
- **Block resources**: `page.route("**/*.{png,jpg,css}", lambda r: r.abort())` for speed.
- **Browser contexts**: isolated profiles with their own cookies; `context.storage_state()` saves a login for reuse.
- **Codegen**: `playwright codegen URL` records your clicks and writes the script.

Use async (`async_playwright`) when scraping many pages concurrently.
keyPoints: Auto-waiting makes scripts more reliable than Selenium sleeps

Block images/CSS with page.route for speed

examples.code:
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

rows = []
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch(headless=True)
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.route("**/*.{png,jpg,jpeg,gif,css}", lambda route: route.abort())

    page.goto("https://quotes.toscrape.com/js/")
    while True:
        page.wait_for_selector("div.quote")
        for q in page.locator("div.quote").all():
            rows.append({
                "text": q.locator("span.text").inner_text(),
                "author": q.locator("small.author").inner_text(),
            })
        next_btn = page.locator("li.next a")
        if next_btn.count() == 0:
            break
        next_btn.click()
    browser.close()

print(len(rows), rows[0])

interview.a: Playwright has auto-waiting, faster execution, built-in network interception and multi-browser contexts; Selenium has a larger legacy ecosystem and language support.

interview.q: How can Playwright help you avoid parsing HTML?
interview.a: By listening to page.on("response") you can capture the JSON API responses the page itself fetches and use them directly.

topics.title: Scrapy: Spiders and Selectors
topics.summary: A full crawling framework: projects, spiders, selectors, following links and exporting data.
topics.description:
**Scrapy** is an asynchronous framework built for large crawls. It handles request scheduling, concurrency, retries, throttling, de-duplication, and exports, so you write only the extraction logic.

```bash
pip install scrapy
scrapy startproject bookscraper
cd bookscraper
scrapy genspider books books.toscrape.com
scrapy crawl books -O books.json
```

### Project layout
`spiders/` (your crawlers), `items.py`, `pipelines.py`, `middlewares.py`, `settings.py`.

### Spider anatomy
- `name`: unique spider name.
- `start_urls`: where to begin.
- `parse(self, response)`: callback receiving a response; `yield` dicts/Items to output and `yield` Requests to follow links.
- `response.css()` and `response.xpath()` return selectors; `.get()` returns the first value and `.getall()` a list.
- `response.follow(url_or_selector, callback)` follows links (handles relative URLs).

### Useful features
- `scrapy shell URL` to experiment interactively.
- Feed exports to JSON, JSONL, CSV, XML with `-O file` (overwrite) or `-o` (append).
- Spider arguments: `scrapy crawl books -a category=travel`.
- `CrawlSpider` with `Rule`/`LinkExtractor` for site-wide crawling.
- Built-in AutoThrottle, retry, cookies and HTTP cache.

### When to choose Scrapy
Many pages, structured pipelines, need for speed and robustness. For a one-off page, `requests` + BeautifulSoup is simpler.

interview.q: What is the difference between yield item and yield Request?
interview.a: Yielding a dict or Item sends data to the item pipeline and exporters; yielding a Request schedules another page to crawl with a callback.

topics.title: Scrapy: Items, Pipelines and Middlewares
topics.summary: Clean and store scraped data with pipelines, and customise requests with middlewares and settings.
topics.description:
### Items
An `Item` (or a `dataclass`) defines the fields your spider outputs. It adds structure and catches typos in field names.

### Item pipelines
After a spider yields an item it passes through the pipelines in order. Each pipeline can **clean**, **validate**, **drop**, **deduplicate** or **store** it.

```python
class CleanPricePipeline:
    def process_item(self, item, spider):
        item["price"] = float(item["price"].replace("£", ""))
        return item
```
Raise `scrapy.exceptions.DropItem` to discard. Enable in `settings.py` with an order number (low runs first):
```python
ITEM_PIPELINES = {
    "bookscraper.pipelines.CleanPricePipeline": 300,
    "bookscraper.pipelines.SQLitePipeline": 800,
}
```
`open_spider` and `close_spider` hooks open and close resources such as DB connections. (Newer Scrapy versions pass fewer arguments; check your version's docs for the exact signatures.)

### Middlewares
- **Downloader middlewares** sit between engine and downloader: modify requests (headers, proxies) and responses (retry, decode). Methods: `process_request`, `process_response`, `process_exception`.
- **Spider middlewares** sit between engine and spiders: filter or alter responses and results.

### Key settings
`ROBOTSTXT_OBEY`, `DOWNLOAD_DELAY`, `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS`, `AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED`, `USER_AGENT`, `RETRY_TIMES`, `HTTPCACHE_ENABLED`, `DEFAULT_REQUEST_HEADERS`, `FEEDS`.

Use pipelines for data work and middlewares for request/response plumbing.

DropItem discards bad items

interview.a: Post-processing scraped items: cleaning, validation, deduplication and saving to files or databases.

interview.q: Difference between downloader and spider middleware?
interview.a: Downloader middleware handles requests/responses around the HTTP download (headers, proxies, retries); spider middleware handles the input to and output from spiders.

topics.title: Saving Scraped Data: CSV, JSON and Databases
topics.summary: Persist results to CSV, JSON lines, SQLite and other stores, and avoid duplicates.
topics.description:
Scraped data is only useful once stored in a clean, queryable form.

### CSV
Best for flat tables and spreadsheets. Use `csv.DictWriter` and `newline=""`, `encoding="utf-8"` (or `utf-8-sig` so Excel shows non-English text correctly).

### JSON / JSON Lines
Use JSON for nested data. For large crawls prefer **JSON Lines** (`.jsonl`): one JSON object per line, appendable and streamable, so a crash does not corrupt the whole file.

### SQLite
A zero-setup SQL database in the standard library: perfect for scrapers. Use a **primary key or UNIQUE constraint** and `INSERT OR REPLACE` / `ON CONFLICT` to avoid duplicates when you re-run. Use parameterised queries (`?`) rather than string formatting.

### Other stores
PostgreSQL/MySQL via SQLAlchemy or psycopg, MongoDB for schemaless documents, pandas `to_csv`/`to_excel`/`to_sql` for analysis, cloud storage for large files.

### Data cleaning checklist
- Strip whitespace; normalise unicode.
- Convert prices and dates to real types.
- Handle missing values explicitly (`None`).
- Add `scraped_at` timestamp and `source_url`.
- De-duplicate by a stable id.

### Scrapy
Built-in feed exports write JSON/CSV with `-O`, and pipelines handle databases.

### Habit
Write incrementally (append or commit every N rows) so that a failure at page 900 does not lose pages 1-899.

topics.title: Anti-Bot Basics and Staying Reliable
topics.summary: Why sites block scrapers and the legitimate techniques for polite, resilient scraping.
topics.description:
Sites protect themselves from abusive traffic using rate limits, IP reputation, header checks, cookies, JavaScript challenges and CAPTCHAs. The goal of this topic is to **make your scraper behave politely and robustly**, not to defeat security systems.

### Why you get blocked
- Too many requests too fast from one IP.
- Missing or unusual headers (the default `python-requests` User-Agent).
- No cookies / session behaviour like a real visitor.
- Perfectly regular timing.
- Datacenter IP addresses.

### Polite and robust practices
1. **Throttle**: delays between requests, random jitter, low concurrency.
2. **Realistic headers**: a normal `User-Agent`, `Accept-Language`, `Referer`.
3. **Use sessions** so cookies persist.
4. **Exponential backoff** on 429/503; honour `Retry-After`.
5. **Cache** responses and avoid re-fetching unchanged pages; use `If-None-Match`/ETag.
6. **Incremental scraping**: only fetch new items.
7. **Proxies**: rotate through legitimately obtained proxies when load must be spread.
8. **Headless browsers** for sites that require JavaScript.
9. **Monitoring**: log status codes and alert when the parse suddenly returns nothing.

### CAPTCHAs and challenges
A CAPTCHA is an explicit signal that automation is unwelcome. Respect it: look for an API, ask for permission or reduce your rate instead of circumventing it.

### Reliability
Sites change. Write extractors that fail loudly (log and skip a field) and keep a few saved HTML fixtures for tests.

Send realistic headers and keep a session
Back off exponentially on 429/5xx and honour Retry-After
Cache and scrape incrementally

pitfalls: Rotating proxies to hide abusive volume
Retrying instantly in a tight loop

interview.a: Increasing the wait time after each failed attempt (for example 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s) so a struggling server is not hammered and temporary limits can expire.

interview.q: How can you reduce the chance of getting blocked ethically?
interview.a: Slow down, use realistic headers and sessions, cache, honour robots.txt and rate-limit responses, and prefer official APIs.

topics.description:
Let us scrape every book from **books.toscrape.com**, a practice site built for learning. Follow these steps for any project.

### 1. Inspect
Open the page in DevTools. Each book is an `article.product_pod`; the title is in `h3 a[title]`, the price in `p.price_color`, the rating is a class on `p.star-rating`, and the next page is `li.next a`.

### 2. Plan the data
Fields: `title`, `price` (float), `rating` (1-5), `in_stock`, `url`. Output: CSV and SQLite.

### 3. Build in small pieces
- `fetch(url)` with a session, headers, timeout and delay.
- `parse_list(html, page_url)` returns a list of dicts.
- `crawl()` follows the next link with a page cap.
- `save_csv(rows)`.

### 4. Make it robust
Check status codes, guard for missing elements, use `urljoin`, deduplicate by URL and log progress.

### 5. Run and verify
Count rows against the number shown on the site (1000 books), spot-check a few values and re-run to confirm no duplicates are created.

### Next steps
Convert prices with `Decimal`, scrape each detail page for descriptions, schedule the job with cron/Task Scheduler, or port it to Scrapy for speed.

examples.code:
import csv
import time
import requests
from urllib.parse import urljoin
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

START = "https://books.toscrape.com/"
HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; CodeReviseBot/1.0)"}
RATING = {"One": 1, "Two": 2, "Three": 3, "Four": 4, "Five": 5}

def fetch(session, url):
    r = session.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=15)
    r.raise_for_status()
    r.encoding = "utf-8"
    return r.text

def parse_list(html, page_url):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml")
    rows = []
    for card in soup.select("article.product_pod"):
        link = card.select_one("h3 a")
        rating_class = card.select_one("p.star-rating")["class"][1]
        rows.append({
            "title": link["title"],
            "price": float(card.select_one("p.price_color").text.replace("£", "")),
            "rating": RATING[rating_class],
            "in_stock": "In stock" in card.select_one("p.availability").text,
            "url": urljoin(page_url, link["href"]),
        })
    nxt = soup.select_one("li.next a")
    return rows, urljoin(page_url, nxt["href"]) if nxt else None

def crawl(max_pages=50):
    rows, url, pages = [], START, 0
    with requests.Session() as s:
        while url and pages < max_pages:
            html = fetch(s, url)
            page_rows, url = parse_list(html, url)
            rows.extend(page_rows)
            pages += 1
            print(f"page {pages}: {len(rows)} books so far")
            time.sleep(0.5)
    return rows

def save_csv(rows, path="books.csv"):
    with open(path, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(rows)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    data = crawl()
    save_csv(data)
    print(len(data), "books saved; cheapest:", min(data, key=lambda r: r["price"])["title"])

interview.q: How would you structure a scraper for maintainability?
interview.a: Split fetching, parsing, crawling and storage into separate functions, keep selectors in one place, add logging and tests using saved HTML fixtures.

interview.q: How do you verify a scraper worked?
interview.a: Compare record counts with the site, check for missing/duplicate values, sample a few rows manually and monitor for sudden drops after site changes.

topics.title: Flask: Hello World and Routing
topics.summary: Install Flask, run your first app and map URLs to view functions with dynamic routes.
topics.description:
**Flask** is a **micro-framework**: it gives you routing, request handling and templating, and leaves databases, forms and auth to extensions you choose. That makes it small, explicit and easy to learn.

### Install and run
```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install flask
flask --app app run --debug
```
`--debug` enables the auto-reloader and interactive debugger (development only).

### Routing
`@app.route(rule, methods=[...])` registers a **view function** for a URL rule.

- Static: `@app.route("/about")`
- Dynamic: `@app.route("/user/<username>")`
- Typed converters: `<int:id>`, `<float:x>`, `<path:subpath>`, `<uuid:id>`
- Methods: default is `GET`; add `methods=["GET", "POST"]`. Shortcuts `@app.get()` and `@app.post()` exist.

### Return values
A view returns a string (HTML), a `dict` (auto-JSON), a tuple `(body, status, headers)` or a `Response` object.

### url_for
Build URLs from endpoint names instead of hard-coding: `url_for("profile", username="asha")`. If you rename a route, links keep working.

### Errors
`abort(404)` raises an HTTP error; `@app.errorhandler(404)` returns a custom page.

### Request lifecycle

Flask exposes the incoming HTTP request through the global-looking `request` proxy (it is context-local and safe per request).

### Reading input
| Source | Access |
|---|---|
| Query string `?q=py` | `request.args.get("q")` |
| HTML form fields | `request.form["name"]` / `.get()` |
| JSON body | `request.get_json()` |
| Uploaded files | `request.files["photo"]` |
| Headers | `request.headers["User-Agent"]` |
| Cookies | `request.cookies.get("theme")` |
| Method, URL | `request.method`, `request.path`, `request.url` |

`request.form["x"]` raises `400 Bad Request` if missing; prefer `.get("x")` when optional.

### Building responses
- Return a string, dict or `jsonify(...)`.
- Set status: `return {"error": "not found"}, 404`.
- `make_response(...)` lets you add headers and cookies: `resp.set_cookie("theme", "dark")`.
- `redirect(url_for("home"))` sends a 302.
- `send_file`, `send_from_directory` for downloads.

### Post/Redirect/Get
After handling a POST, redirect to a GET page so a browser refresh does not resubmit the form.

### Flash messages
`flash("Saved!")` stores a one-time message in the session; show it with `get_flashed_messages()`.

### File uploads
Always use `werkzeug.utils.secure_filename`, restrict extensions and size (`MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH`).

topics.title: Flask: Forms and Validation with WTForms
topics.summary: Build validated, CSRF-protected forms using Flask-WTF.
topics.description:
Handling forms by hand means repeating parsing, validation, error messages and CSRF protection. **Flask-WTF** (WTForms plus CSRF) turns a form into a class.

```bash
pip install flask-wtf email-validator
```

### Defining a form
```python
from flask_wtf import FlaskForm
from wtforms import StringField, PasswordField, SubmitField
from wtforms.validators import DataRequired, Email, Length, EqualTo

class RegisterForm(FlaskForm):
    email = StringField("Email", validators=[DataRequired(), Email()])
    password = PasswordField("Password", validators=[DataRequired(), Length(min=8)])
    confirm = PasswordField("Confirm", validators=[EqualTo("password")])
    submit = SubmitField("Register")
```

### In the view
`form.validate_on_submit()` is `True` only for a POST whose data passes all validators and the CSRF check. Errors are available in `form.errors` and per field in `form.email.errors`.

### In the template
```html
<form method="post">
  {{ form.hidden_tag() }}   <!-- CSRF token -->
  {{ form.email.label }} {{ form.email() }}
  {% for e in form.email.errors %}<small>{{ e }}</small>{% endfor %}
  {{ form.submit() }}
</form>
```

### Why CSRF protection?
Cross-Site Request Forgery tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request. A per-session secret token in each form prevents it; this requires `SECRET_KEY`.

### Custom validators
Add `validate_<fieldname>(self, field)` methods to a form class to check uniqueness or business rules and raise `ValidationError`.

Always validate on the **server**, even if you also validate in JavaScript.

topics.title: Flask: Blueprints and the App Factory
topics.summary: Organise a growing Flask app into modules with blueprints and an application factory.
topics.description:
A single `app.py` becomes unmanageable as an app grows. Two patterns keep things organised.

### Blueprints
A **Blueprint** is a bundle of routes, templates and static files that can be registered on an app, often with a URL prefix. Think of it as a mini-app: `auth`, `blog`, `api`.

```python
# blog/routes.py
from flask import Blueprint
bp = Blueprint("blog", __name__, url_prefix="/blog", template_folder="templates")

@bp.route("/")
def index(): ...
```
Endpoint names become `blog.index`, so `url_for("blog.index")`.

### Application factory
Create the app inside a function so you can build different instances (development, testing) and avoid circular imports.

```python
def create_app(config_object="config.DevConfig"):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config.from_object(config_object)
    db.init_app(app)
    from .blog.routes import bp as blog_bp
    app.register_blueprint(blog_bp)
    return app
```
Extensions are created without an app (`db = SQLAlchemy()`) and attached with `init_app`.

### Typical layout
```text
myapp/
  __init__.py      # create_app
  extensions.py    # db, login_manager
  models.py
  auth/ routes.py forms.py
  blog/ routes.py
  templates/
  tests/
```

### Benefits
Separation of concerns, easier testing (`create_app("config.TestConfig")`), reuse of blueprints across projects and cleaner team collaboration.

Endpoints are prefixed: url_for("blog.index")

bp = Blueprint("api", __name__, url_prefix="/api/v1")

topics.title: Flask: Databases with SQLAlchemy
topics.summary: Define models and query a database with Flask-SQLAlchemy and run migrations.
topics.description:
**SQLAlchemy** is Python's best-known ORM (object-relational mapper): you work with classes and objects instead of raw SQL. **Flask-SQLAlchemy** integrates it with Flask.

```bash
pip install flask-sqlalchemy flask-migrate
```

### Setup
```python
app.config["SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI"] = "sqlite:///app.db"
db = SQLAlchemy(model_class=Base)
db.init_app(app)
```
Use `postgresql+psycopg://user:pw@host/db` for PostgreSQL.

### Models
A model class maps to a table; attributes map to columns. Relationships (`relationship`, `ForeignKey`) link tables.

### Queries (SQLAlchemy 2.0 style)
- Select: `db.session.execute(db.select(User).where(User.email == e)).scalar_one_or_none()`
- All: `db.session.scalars(db.select(Post).order_by(Post.id.desc())).all()`
- By primary key: `db.session.get(User, 1)` or `db.get_or_404(User, 1)`
- Paginate: `db.paginate(db.select(Post), page=1, per_page=10)`
- Write: `db.session.add(obj)`, `db.session.delete(obj)`, then `db.session.commit()`.

### Migrations
Use **Flask-Migrate** (Alembic): `flask db init`, `flask db migrate -m "add posts"`, `flask db upgrade`. Never rely on `create_all()` for schema changes in a real project.

### Good habits
Commit once per request, roll back on error, avoid the N+1 query problem with `selectinload`/`joinedload`, and keep secrets out of the URI by reading from environment variables.

examples.code:
from flask import Flask, jsonify, request
from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, String
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

db = SQLAlchemy(model_class=Base)
app = Flask(__name__)
app.config["SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI"] = "sqlite:///blog.db"
db.init_app(app)

class User(db.Model):
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    username: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50), unique=True)
    posts: Mapped[list["Post"]] = relationship(back_populates="author")

class Post(db.Model):
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(120))
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("user.id"))
    author: Mapped[User] = relationship(back_populates="posts")

with app.app_context():
    db.create_all()

@app.post("/posts")
def create_post():
    data = request.get_json()
    user = db.session.scalar(db.select(User).where(User.username == data["author"]))
    if user is None:
        user = User(username=data["author"])
        db.session.add(user)
    post = Post(title=data["title"], author=user)
    db.session.add(post)
    db.session.commit()
    return jsonify(id=post.id), 201

@app.get("/posts")
def list_posts():
    posts = db.session.scalars(db.select(Post).order_by(Post.id.desc())).all()
    return jsonify([{"id": p.id, "title": p.title, "author": p.author.username} for p in posts])

interview.a: An Object-Relational Mapper maps database tables to classes and rows to objects so you query and modify data with Python code instead of hand-written SQL.

interview.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
interview.a: Loading a list then issuing one extra query per item to fetch a related object; fix with eager loading (joinedload/selectinload).

topics.title: Flask: Building a REST API
topics.summary: Design JSON endpoints with correct methods, status codes, validation and error handling.
topics.description:
A **REST API** exposes resources (users, posts) at URLs and uses HTTP methods as verbs.

| Action | Method | URL | Success code |
|---|---|---|---|
| List | GET | `/api/tasks` | 200 |
| Create | POST | `/api/tasks` | 201 |
| Read one | GET | `/api/tasks/5` | 200 |
| Update | PUT / PATCH | `/api/tasks/5` | 200 |
| Delete | DELETE | `/api/tasks/5` | 204 |

### Principles
- Nouns in URLs, verbs via methods.
- Return JSON and use meaningful **status codes**: 400 invalid input, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 422 validation error.
- Be **stateless**: each request carries what the server needs (token in header).
- Version the API (`/api/v1/`) and paginate lists.

### In Flask
Use `jsonify`, `request.get_json()`, `abort`, and a JSON error handler so errors are not HTML pages. For larger projects use **Flask-RESTX**, **Flask-Smorest** or **marshmallow** for schemas, validation and OpenAPI docs.

### Validation
Never trust the input. Check required keys and types and return `400` with a clear message. Marshmallow or Pydantic schemas centralise this.

### CORS
Browsers block cross-origin calls unless the server sends CORS headers; add `flask-cors` for front-end apps hosted on another origin.

### Testing
`app.test_client().post("/api/tasks", json={...})` makes testing simple with pytest.

topics.title: Flask: Sessions and Authentication
topics.summary: Hash passwords, keep users logged in with sessions, and protect routes with Flask-Login.
topics.description:
### Sessions
`flask.session` is a dict-like object stored in a **signed cookie**. Flask signs it with `SECRET_KEY` so users cannot tamper with it, but its contents are readable, so never store secrets there. For server-side sessions use `Flask-Session`.

### Password storage
Never store plain passwords. Hash them with a slow, salted algorithm:
```python
from werkzeug.security import generate_password_hash, check_password_hash
user.password_hash = generate_password_hash(password)
check_password_hash(user.password_hash, attempt)
```

### Flask-Login
Manages the logged-in user across requests.
- `LoginManager` with `login_view = "auth.login"`.
- `UserMixin` on the model supplies `is_authenticated` etc.
- `@login_manager.user_loader` loads a user from the id stored in the session.
- `login_user(user, remember=True)`, `logout_user()`, `current_user`, `@login_required`.

### Token-based auth for APIs
Browsers use cookies; APIs and mobile apps typically send `Authorization: Bearer <JWT>`. Extensions: `Flask-JWT-Extended`.

### Security checklist
- Hash passwords; never log them.
- `SECRET_KEY` from the environment, long and random.
- `SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY`, `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE`, `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax"`.
- CSRF protection on every state-changing form.
- Use HTTPS in production, rate-limit login attempts, validate `next` redirects.

Flask-Login provides login_user, logout_user, @login_required
Use JWT/bearer tokens for APIs

interview.q: Why hash passwords instead of encrypting them?
interview.a: Hashing is one-way, so a database leak does not reveal passwords; salted slow hashes also resist brute-force attacks.

topics.title: Flask: Configuration and Deployment
topics.summary: Manage settings per environment and deploy with gunicorn, a reverse proxy and Docker.
topics.description:
### Configuration
`app.config` is a dict. Load it from objects, files or the environment:
```python
class Config:
    SECRET_KEY = os.environ["SECRET_KEY"]
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = os.environ.get("DATABASE_URL", "sqlite:///app.db")
class ProdConfig(Config):
    DEBUG = False
class TestConfig(Config):
    TESTING = True
app.config.from_object("config.ProdConfig")
```
Keep **secrets out of source control**: use environment variables or a `.env` file loaded with `python-dotenv` (Flask does this automatically for `.flaskenv`/`.env`). Follow the 12-factor idea: same code, different config per environment.

### Why not `flask run` in production?
The built-in server is single-purpose for development. Use a production **WSGI server**.

### gunicorn
```bash
pip install gunicorn
gunicorn -w 4 -b 0.0.0.0:8000 "myapp:create_app()"
```
Workers = roughly `2 * cores + 1`. On Windows use `waitress` instead.

### Reverse proxy
Put **Nginx** (or a cloud load balancer) in front of gunicorn to terminate HTTPS, serve static files and buffer slow clients. Behind a proxy use `ProxyFix` so Flask sees the real scheme and client IP.

### Docker
Package the app in a container: a `Dockerfile` that installs requirements and starts gunicorn.

### Checklist
`DEBUG=False`, strong `SECRET_KEY`, HTTPS, logging, database migrations run on deploy, a health endpoint, and process supervision (systemd, Docker restart policies).

topics.title: Django: Project Structure, Apps and MTV
topics.summary: Understand what Django is, create a project and apps, and learn the Model-Template-View pattern.
topics.description:
**Django** is a "batteries-included" web framework: ORM, admin, authentication, forms, templates, security protections, migrations and more come in the box. It follows the **MTV** pattern.

### MTV
| Part | Role | Files |
|---|---|---|
| **Model** | data and business rules (database tables) | `models.py` |
| **Template** | presentation (HTML) | `templates/` |
| **View** | request handling logic, glues model and template | `views.py` |

The **URLconf** (`urls.py`) routes a URL to a view. (It is the same idea as MVC, with the framework itself acting as the controller.)

### Start a project
```bash
pip install django
django-admin startproject mysite
cd mysite
python manage.py startapp blog
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py runserver
```

### Project vs app
A **project** is the whole website (settings, root URLs, WSGI/ASGI entry points). An **app** is a reusable feature module (`blog`, `accounts`, `shop`). One project contains many apps; register each in `INSTALLED_APPS`.

### Layout
```text
mysite/
  manage.py
  mysite/ settings.py urls.py asgi.py wsgi.py
  blog/ models.py views.py urls.py admin.py apps.py forms.py tests.py migrations/
  templates/
```

### Request flow
Request -> middleware -> URL resolver -> view -> (ORM/models) -> template -> response -> middleware -> client.

### manage.py commands
`runserver`, `makemigrations`, `migrate`, `createsuperuser`, `shell`, `test`, `collectstatic`, `check`.

topics.title: Django: Models and the ORM
topics.summary: Define database tables as Python classes, relate them and query with QuerySets.
topics.description:
A **model** is a class that subclasses `models.Model`; each attribute is a column. Django's **ORM** generates SQL for you and works with SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and others.

### Fields
`CharField(max_length=...)`, `TextField`, `IntegerField`, `DecimalField`, `BooleanField`, `DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)`, `SlugField`, `EmailField`, `FileField`, `ImageField`, `JSONField`.

### Relationships
- `ForeignKey` many-to-one (`on_delete=models.CASCADE / SET_NULL / PROTECT`).
- `ManyToManyField`.
- `OneToOneField`.
Use `related_name` to name the reverse accessor.

### Meta and methods
`class Meta: ordering, indexes, constraints, verbose_name`. Add `__str__` and `get_absolute_url`.

### QuerySets
A QuerySet is **lazy**: no database hit until you iterate, slice with a step, call `list()`, `len()` or evaluate it.

```python
Post.objects.all()
Post.objects.filter(status="published", title__icontains="django")
Post.objects.exclude(author=user).order_by("-created_at")[:10]
Post.objects.get(pk=1)            # raises DoesNotExist / MultipleObjectsReturned
Post.objects.create(title="Hi", author=user)
post.save(); post.delete()
```
Field lookups use double underscores: `__gt`, `__in`, `__contains`, `__startswith`, `__isnull`, `author__username="asha"`.

### Custom managers

topics.title: Django: Migrations
topics.summary: Version-control your database schema with makemigrations and migrate.
topics.description:
**Migrations** are Django's way of propagating model changes (new field, new table, removed column) to the database schema. They are Python files stored in each app's `migrations/` folder, committed to git like source code.

### The two commands
```bash
python manage.py makemigrations     # generates migration files from model changes
python manage.py migrate            # applies unapplied migrations to the database
```
Each migration has dependencies, so Django applies them in the right order.

### Other useful commands
- `showmigrations`: list applied/unapplied.
- `sqlmigrate blog 0002`: show the SQL.
- `migrate blog 0001`: roll back to a previous migration.
- `makemigrations --empty app`: create a blank one for data migrations.
- `squashmigrations`: combine many into one.

### Data migrations
Use `RunPython(forward, backward)` to transform existing data, for example filling a new field from an old one.

### Adding fields to existing tables
A new non-null field needs a `default` (or `null=True`), otherwise Django asks for a one-off default because existing rows must get a value.

### Good practices
- Commit migrations; never edit applied ones in shared environments.
- Run `migrate` on every deployment.
- Make big changes in small steps (add nullable column -> backfill -> make required).
- When a team merges two branches that both added migrations, run `makemigrations --merge`.
- Create a custom user model **before** the first migrate.

# data migration skeleton

def fill_slugs(apps, schema_editor):
    Post = apps.get_model("blog", "Post")
    for p in Post.objects.filter(slug=""):
        p.slug = f"post-{p.pk}"
        p.save(update_fields=["slug"])

class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [("blog", "0002_post_views_count")]
    operations = [migrations.RunPython(fill_slugs, migrations.RunPython.noop)]

topics.title: Django: Function and Class-Based Views
topics.summary: Handle requests with function-based views or reusable generic class-based views.
topics.description:
A **view** takes an `HttpRequest` and returns an `HttpResponse` (HTML, JSON, redirect, file).

### Function-based views (FBV)
Simple and explicit. Great for custom logic.

```python
def post_list(request):
    posts = Post.objects.filter(status="published")
    return render(request, "blog/list.html", {"posts": posts})
```
Helpers: `render`, `redirect`, `get_object_or_404`, `JsonResponse`, `HttpResponseBadRequest`.

### Class-based views (CBV)
A class with methods per HTTP verb (`get`, `post`). Django ships **generic views** that implement common patterns:

| View | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ListView` | list objects (with pagination) |
| `DetailView` | one object |
| `CreateView` | form + create |
| `UpdateView` | form + update |
| `DeleteView` | confirm + delete |
| `TemplateView` | static template |

Customise through attributes (`model`, `template_name`, `paginate_by`, `context_object_name`) and by overriding methods (`get_queryset`, `get_context_data`, `form_valid`).

### Mixins
`LoginRequiredMixin`, `PermissionRequiredMixin`, `UserPassesTestMixin` add behaviour; put them **before** the view class in the inheritance list.

### FBV or CBV?
CBVs remove boilerplate for CRUD pages; FBVs are easier to read for unusual logic. Many teams mix both. Always handle the "not found" case with `get_object_or_404`.

### Decorators
`@login_required`, `@require_POST`, `@permission_required`, `@csrf_exempt` (avoid unless you know why).

FBVs are explicit; CBVs reuse generic CRUD behaviour

examples.code:
from django.contrib.auth.mixins import LoginRequiredMixin
from django.shortcuts import render, get_object_or_404, redirect
from django.views.generic import ListView, DetailView, CreateView
from .models import Post
from .forms import PostForm

# function-based
def post_detail(request, slug):
    post = get_object_or_404(Post, slug=slug, status="published")
    return render(request, "blog/detail.html", {"post": post})

# class-based
class PostListView(ListView):
    model = Post
    template_name = "blog/list.html"
    context_object_name = "posts"
    paginate_by = 10

    def get_queryset(self):
        qs = super().get_queryset().filter(status="published").select_related("author")
        q = self.request.GET.get("q")
        return qs.filter(title__icontains=q) if q else qs

class PostCreateView(LoginRequiredMixin, CreateView):
    model = Post
    form_class = PostForm
    template_name = "blog/form.html"

    def form_valid(self, form):
        form.instance.author = self.request.user
        return super().form_valid(form)

topics.title: Django: URL Routing
topics.summary: Map URLs to views with path(), converters, include() and namespaces.
topics.description:
The **URLconf** is a list called `urlpatterns` of `path()` entries, checked top to bottom until one matches.

```python
from django.urls import path, include
from . import views

app_name = "blog"                       # namespace

urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.PostListView.as_view(), name="list"),
    path("<slug:slug>/", views.post_detail, name="detail"),
    path("<int:year>/<int:month>/", views.archive, name="archive"),
]
```

### Converters
`str`, `int`, `slug`, `uuid`, `path`. Captured values are passed to the view as keyword arguments. Use `re_path()` for regex patterns and custom converters for special formats.

### include()
The root `urls.py` delegates to apps: `path("blog/", include("blog.urls"))`. This keeps each app self-contained and lets you mount it anywhere.

### Naming and reversing
Always give routes a `name` and **reverse** them instead of hard-coding:

- Python: `reverse("blog:detail", kwargs={"slug": "intro"})`
- Template: `{% url 'blog:detail' slug=post.slug %}`

### Namespaces
`app_name` plus `include` produce names such as `blog:detail`, avoiding collisions between apps.

### Serving media and static in development
```python
if settings.DEBUG:
    urlpatterns += static(settings.MEDIA_URL, document_root=settings.MEDIA_ROOT)
```

### Order matters
Put specific patterns before generic ones such as `<slug:slug>/`, which would otherwise swallow `create/`.

topics.title: Django: Forms and ModelForms
topics.summary: Validate input and render HTML forms with Form and ModelForm classes.
topics.description:
Django forms handle three jobs: **render** HTML inputs, **validate** submitted data and **convert** it to Python types.

### Form
```python
class ContactForm(forms.Form):
    name = forms.CharField(max_length=80)
    email = forms.EmailField()
    message = forms.CharField(widget=forms.Textarea)
```

### ModelForm
Generated from a model, so field definitions and validation are not duplicated:
```python
class PostForm(forms.ModelForm):
    class Meta:
        model = Post
        fields = ["title", "slug", "category", "body"]
```
`form.save()` creates or updates the model instance. Always list `fields` explicitly (never `__all__` with sensitive fields).

### View pattern
```python
form = PostForm(request.POST or None)
if form.is_valid():
    ...
    return redirect(...)
```
`is_valid()` runs validators and fills `form.cleaned_data` (or `form.errors`).

### Validation hooks
- `clean_<field>()` validates one field.
- `clean()` validates across fields.
- Validators on the field: `MinLengthValidator`, `RegexValidator`.

### Rendering
`{{ form.as_p }}`, or loop `{% for field in form %}` with `{{ field.errors }}`. Add CSS classes in the widget `attrs`, or use `django-crispy-forms`.

### File uploads
Use `enctype="multipart/form-data"` and `request.FILES`.

### Formsets
Edit several related objects at once with `modelformset_factory` or inline formsets.

topics.title: Django: The Admin Site
topics.summary: Get a full CRUD back-office for free and customise it with ModelAdmin.
topics.description:
Django's **admin** is an auto-generated back-office built from your models. It is perfect for content editors, internal tools and quick data inspection.

### Enable
`django.contrib.admin` is installed by default. Create an admin user and open `/admin/`:
```bash
python manage.py createsuperuser
```

### Register models
```python
from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Post

@admin.register(Post)
class PostAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ("title", "author", "status", "created_at")
    list_filter = ("status", "created_at", "category")
    search_fields = ("title", "body", "author__username")
    prepopulated_fields = {"slug": ("title",)}
    list_editable = ("status",)
    date_hierarchy = "created_at"
    raw_id_fields = ("author",)
    actions = ["make_published"]

    @admin.action(description="Mark selected as published")
    def make_published(self, request, queryset):
        queryset.update(status="published")
```

### Useful features
- **Inlines** (`TabularInline`, `StackedInline`) edit related objects on the same page.
- `readonly_fields`, `fieldsets`, `ordering`, `list_per_page`.
- Custom columns: methods on the ModelAdmin decorated with `@admin.display`.
- Permissions per model and per action; staff vs superuser.

### Caution
The admin is for trusted staff. Do not expose it as your public user interface, change the URL from `/admin/` in production if desired, and require strong passwords (consider 2FA).

topics.title: Django: Authentication and Permissions
topics.summary: Use the built-in User model, login/logout views, decorators, permissions and custom users.
topics.description:
Django ships a full authentication system: users, groups, permissions, sessions and password hashing.

### Pieces
- `django.contrib.auth.models.User` with `username`, `password` (hashed with PBKDF2 by default), `email`, `is_staff`, `is_superuser`.
- Sessions via `django.contrib.sessions` and the `AuthenticationMiddleware`, which sets `request.user` on every request.
- Ready-made views in `django.contrib.auth.urls`: `login`, `logout`, `password_change`, `password_reset`.

### Using it
```python
user = authenticate(request, username=u, password=p)
if user is not None:
    login(request, user)
logout(request)
```
In views: `request.user.is_authenticated`. In templates: `{{ user.username }}`.

### Protecting views
- FBV: `@login_required`, `@permission_required("blog.add_post")`.
- CBV: `LoginRequiredMixin`, `PermissionRequiredMixin`.
- Settings: `LOGIN_URL`, `LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL`, `LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL`.

### Permissions
Every model gets `add`, `change`, `delete`, `view` permissions automatically. Assign to users or **groups** and check with `user.has_perm("blog.change_post")`. For object-level rules use `django-guardian` or custom checks.

### Custom user model
Set it **at the start of the project**:
```python
class User(AbstractUser):
    phone = models.CharField(max_length=15, blank=True)
# settings.py
AUTH_USER_MODEL = "accounts.User"
```
Always reference `settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL` or `get_user_model()`.

### APIs
For REST APIs use token or JWT authentication through DRF (`SimpleJWT`, `TokenAuthentication`).

topics.title: Django: Middleware and Signals
topics.summary: Run code around every request with middleware, and react to model events with signals.
topics.description:
### Middleware
**Middleware** is a chain of hooks that wraps request processing. Each one can modify the request before the view, the response after it, or short-circuit the pipeline. Typical built-ins: security headers, sessions, CSRF, authentication, messages, clickjacking protection, gzip.

Order in `MIDDLEWARE` matters: requests pass **top to bottom**, responses return **bottom to top**.

### Writing middleware
```python
class TimingMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response      # one-time setup

    def __call__(self, request):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        response = self.get_response(request) # view and inner middleware
        response["X-Time-ms"] = f"{(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.1f}"
        return response
```
Optional hooks: `process_view`, `process_exception`, `process_template_response`. Add the dotted path to `MIDDLEWARE`.

### Use cases
Logging, rate limiting, request IDs, tenant detection, maintenance mode, adding headers, redirecting based on language.

### Signals
Signals let decoupled code react to events: `pre_save`, `post_save`, `post_delete`, `m2m_changed`, `request_finished`.
```python
@receiver(post_save, sender=User)
def create_profile(sender, instance, created, **kwargs):
    if created:
        Profile.objects.create(user=instance)
```
Register them in `AppConfig.ready()`.

### Caution
Signals hide control flow and are hard to debug; prefer explicit service functions or overriding `save()` when practical. Keep middleware fast because it runs on every request.

# core/middleware.py
import logging
import uuid

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

class RequestIDMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.request_id = request.headers.get("X-Request-ID", uuid.uuid4().hex)
        response = self.get_response(request)
        response["X-Request-ID"] = request.request_id
        logger.info("%s %s -> %s [%s]", request.method, request.path,
                    response.status_code, request.request_id)
        return response

# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware",
    "core.middleware.RequestIDMiddleware",
]

topics.title: Django: Advanced ORM and Performance
topics.summary: Use Q, F, annotate, aggregate, select_related and prefetch_related to write fast queries.
topics.description:
Most Django performance problems are database problems. Learn these tools.

### Q objects
Combine conditions with OR / NOT: `Post.objects.filter(Q(title__icontains="py") | Q(body__icontains="py"))`.

### F expressions
Refer to a column in the database itself, avoiding race conditions:
`Post.objects.filter(pk=1).update(views=F("views") + 1)`.

### Aggregation and annotation
- `aggregate()` returns one dict for the whole set: `Post.objects.aggregate(Avg("rating"))`.
- `annotate()` adds a computed value to each row: `Author.objects.annotate(n=Count("posts"))`.
- `values()` / `values_list()` return dicts or tuples, handy with `annotate` for group-by.

### The N+1 problem
Iterating posts and printing `post.author.name` runs one extra query per post.
- `select_related("author")` uses a SQL JOIN (foreign key and one-to-one).
- `prefetch_related("tags")` runs a second query and joins in Python (many-to-many and reverse FK).

### Other optimisations
- `only()` / `defer()` limit columns.
- `exists()` instead of `len(qs) > 0`; `count()` instead of `len(qs)`.
- `bulk_create`, `bulk_update` for many rows.
- `iterator()` for huge result sets.
- Add `db_index=True` or `Meta.indexes` for frequently filtered columns.
- `transaction.atomic()` for all-or-nothing writes.

### Detect problems
`django-debug-toolbar`, `connection.queries`, or `assertNumQueries` in tests.

examples.code:
from django.db import transaction
from django.db.models import Count, Avg, F, Q, Prefetch

# N+1 fixed
posts = (
    Post.objects.filter(status="published")
    .select_related("author", "category")
    .prefetch_related("tags")
)

# OR conditions and ordering
hits = Post.objects.filter(Q(title__icontains="django") | Q(tags__name="python")).distinct()

# group by: posts per author
stats = (
    User.objects.annotate(post_count=Count("posts"))
    .filter(post_count__gt=0)
    .order_by("-post_count")
    .values("username", "post_count")
)

# atomic counter increment
Post.objects.filter(pk=7).update(views=F("views") + 1)

# prefetch with a filtered queryset
authors = User.objects.prefetch_related(
    Prefetch("posts", queryset=Post.objects.filter(status="published"), to_attr="live_posts")
)

with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.create(user=user)
    OrderItem.objects.bulk_create([OrderItem(order=order, product=p) for p in products])

interview.a: select_related performs a SQL JOIN for single-valued relations in one query; prefetch_related does a separate query and joins in Python for many-valued relations.
They let the database perform the calculation on its own value, which avoids race conditions and extra queries.

topics.title: Django REST Framework (DRF)
topics.summary: Build JSON APIs with serializers, viewsets, routers, authentication and permissions.
topics.description:
**Django REST Framework** turns Django models into full-featured REST APIs.

```bash
pip install djangorestframework
# add "rest_framework" to INSTALLED_APPS
```

### Serializers
Convert model instances to JSON and validate incoming JSON. `ModelSerializer` generates fields automatically.
```python
class PostSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    author = serializers.StringRelatedField(read_only=True)
    class Meta:
        model = Post
        fields = ["id", "title", "body", "author", "created_at"]
```
Custom validation with `validate_<field>()` and `validate()`.

### Views
- `APIView` (class-based, explicit).
- Generic views: `ListCreateAPIView`, `RetrieveUpdateDestroyAPIView`.
- **ViewSets** group list/create/retrieve/update/destroy in one class; `ModelViewSet` gives full CRUD.

### Routers
`DefaultRouter` generates the URLs for a viewset automatically.

### Auth and permissions
Authentication classes: Session, Token, JWT (SimpleJWT). Permission classes: `IsAuthenticated`, `IsAdminUser`, `IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly`, or custom `BasePermission` (e.g. `IsOwner`).

### Extras
Pagination (`PageNumberPagination`), filtering (`django-filter`), throttling, versioning, and the **browsable API** for testing in the browser. Use `drf-spectacular` for OpenAPI/Swagger docs.

### Performance
Use `select_related`/`prefetch_related` in `get_queryset` to avoid N+1 queries in nested serialization.
keyPoints: Serializers convert and validate data
ModelViewSet + Router gives CRUD with little code
Permission classes protect endpoints
Pagination, filtering and throttling are built in
Optimise get_queryset with select_related/prefetch_related
pitfalls: Nested serializers causing N+1 queries
Forgetting permission classes (default allows any)
Exposing all fields with fields = "__all__"
